newsitem.title: CHINA: Paramilitary in China village over election row.
newsitem.headline: Paramilitary in China village over election row.

text.p: Chinese authorities have sent hundreds of paramilitary armed police to restore order in a mountain town in southern Guangdong after a dispute over local elections turned violent, local officials said on Sunday.
"There was a situation of no government," one local official said by telephone from the town of Wuyun.

Local officials said recent protests, which grew violent, in Wuyun were a result of a string of disputes that had built up over several years, including rows over land and the recent failure of local authorities to announce village election results.
Several officials sent in from neighbouring areas last week to take over administration of the restive region were beaten up by angry local residents, said one government official.

Officials of nearby Jieyang city sent about 100 police troopers into Wuyun village early on Saturday and the provincial government mobilised more than 500 paramilitary People's Armed Police to restore order, one Wuyun public security official said.

The latest unrest erupted in the mountain town about 325 km (195 miles) east of the Guangdong provincial capital of Guangzhou when Jieyang authorities sent work teams to Wuyun last week to take over management of the village from the local government, the official said.
The work teams fanned out into about five smaller mountain villages around Wuyun, an area with a population of about 30,000, local officials said.

"Some unknown people led the villagers to start agitation," said the government official, apparently a member of one of the work teams from Jieyang. "A few people from the working groups were beaten up."
However, no one was seriously injured, he said.
Villagers were angered by the failure of the Wuyun government to announce the results of local village elections, he said.

"They could not announce the names of elected delegates or the name of who was elected as village chief," the official said, hinting at a local power struggle with officials unhappy with some election results.
"They did not even announce the names of any elected representatives."
China has introduced a system of grassroots village elections by which farmers can elect their local government representatives in multi-candidate polls.

While in many areas villagers elect existing local leaders, seeing them as representing stability, the system has also raised the possibility that local vested interests who lose the confidence of their electorate can lose their positions.
Elections in southern Guangdong are also complicated by the powerbase of local clans.
Some of the violent demonstrations in Wuyun erupted after supporters of ousted local government officials protested against the arrival of the working group, the official said.
The area was now calm, he said.
